title: Tracing Persona Vectors Through LLM Pretraining
claim: Target behavioral representations become effective for steering very early in training and remain stable and usable through later training stages.
layout: 2 stacked panels sharing x-axis; line plots with shaded training-phase background regions
description: A two-panel line chart sharing a log-scale x-axis of source checkpoints, running from 4B tokens to 6.1T tokens and then SFT, DPO and RLVR. Background shading marks Pretraining (blue), Midtraining (tan) and Post-training (green). The large top panel plots the steering effect (Δτ) for four traits, each in its own colour: evil in orange, humorous in blue, impolite in magenta and sycophantic in green. Star markers show significant points. The traits rise from near zero to roughly 10–40 and fluctuate, with sycophancy spiking near 415B tokens. A grey strip below zero holds × markers (incoherent outputs) and + markers (no persona) at the earliest checkpoints. The bottom panel shows pass rate rising from about 0 to 40% and then plateauing. The eye goes first to the colourful jagged lines in the top panel.
caption: Personas emerge early and stay stable throughout OLMo-3 7B pretraining. Top: For each trait, the persona vector is extracted at checkpoint $M_r$ and applied to steer the same checkpoint. The $y$-axis reports the trait-expression delta $\Delta_\tau$ (steered $-$ baseline; higher = stronger steering effect). Bottom: pass rate at $M_r$ --- the fraction of generations whose trait score $\geq 50$. The shared $x$-axis shows checkpoints as pretraining tokens consumed up to $M_r$. Bottom-side markers flag checkpoints where no vector could be built ($\times$: outputs not coherent; $+$: outputs fail to express persona).
abstract: How large language models internally represent high-level behaviors is a core interpretability question with direct relevance to AI safety: it determines what we can detect, audit, or intervene on. Recent work has shown that traits such as evil or sycophancy correspond to linear directions in the internal activations, the so-called persona vectors. Although these vectors are now routinely utilized to inspect and steer model behavior in safety-relevant settings, how these representations are formed during training remains unknown. To address this gap, we trace persona vectors across the pretraining of OLMo-3-7B, finding that persona vectors form remarkably early -- within 0.22% of OLMo-3 pretraining -- and remain effective for steering the fully post-trained instruct models. Although core representations are formed early on, persona vectors continue to refine geometrically and semantically throughout pretraining. We further compare alternative elicitation strategies and find that all yield effective directions, with each strategy surfacing qualitatively distinct facets of the underlying persona. Replicating our analysis on Apertus-8B reveals that our findings transfer qualitatively beyond OLMo-3. Our results establish persona representations as stable features of early pretraining and open a path to studying how training forms, refines, and shapes them.
